## In 60 seconds

A model that scores well on average can still mislead: its explanation may not reflect what it computes, its
confidence may be wrong for one class or one group of patients, it may be applied to recordings unlike its
training data, and small changes to the input can flip its output. This module builds a tool for each concern.
Integrated gradients attribute an output to the samples of an ECG, and a randomization test checks that the
attribution depends on the model [@sundararajan2017ig; @adebayo2018sanity]. Conformal prediction turns scores into
sets with a coverage guarantee [@angelopoulos2021conformal]. Group metrics show why equal error rates and equal
predictive values cannot both hold when prevalences differ [@chouldechova2017], as AI-ECG studies across race,
sex and age illustrate [@noseworthy2020; @kaur2023]. A Mahalanobis score flags unfamiliar inputs
[@lee2018mahalanobis], and adversarial examples show how fragile an ECG classifier can be
[@han2020; @goodfellow2015fgsm].

## From the field

- **Explanations on the 12-lead ECG.** A network trained on 992,748 ECGs from 365,009 patients reached an AUC of
  at least 0.960 for 32 of 38 classes in its test set, and a local-surrogate explanation method (LIME) highlighted
  physiologically relevant ECG segments [@hughes2021]. At Stanford, interpretation analyses of an echocardiography network showed
  attention to the relevant cardiac structures for tasks people can check, and highlighted regions for tasks they
  cannot, such as predicting age and sex [@ghorbani2020].
- **Performance by race, sex and age.** A network that detects low ejection fraction from the ECG, derived in a
  cohort that was 96.2% non-Hispanic white, kept AUCs between 0.931 and 0.961 across racial and ethnic subgroups
  of its test cohort; a separate network could predict racial category from the ECG, and the authors recommended
  reporting performance by race, ethnicity, age and sex [@noseworthy2020]. A Stanford heart-failure model showed
  no significant difference between racial groups overall but performed worse in young Black patients, most of
  all young Black women; adding demographics to the model, training separate models or balancing the data did not
  remove the gap, and group-specific thresholds improved F1 [@kaur2023].
- **Attacks that experts cannot see.** Smoothed adversarial perturbations fooled a single-lead arrhythmia network
  while remaining invisible to expert review; the authors advise care where there is an incentive to alter ECGs
  [@han2020].
- **Reporting.** The EHRA, HRS and ESC statement found key items such as participant details and data handling
  under-reported in AI-in-EP studies [@svennberg2025] (m45).

## Derivations

### Explanations: integrated gradients

For a model output $F(\mathbf x)$, an input $\mathbf x$ (for example the samples of a beat) and a baseline
$\mathbf x'$ (a flat line), integrated gradients attribute to sample $i$ [@sundararajan2017ig]

$$
\mathrm{IG}_i(\mathbf x) = (x_i - x'_i)\int_0^1 \frac{\partial F\bigl(\mathbf x' + \alpha(\mathbf x - \mathbf x')\bigr)}{\partial x_i}\,d\alpha,
\qquad \sum_i \mathrm{IG}_i(\mathbf x) = F(\mathbf x) - F(\mathbf x')
$$ {#eq-m46-ig}

The second identity, completeness, is the fundamental theorem of calculus along the path; checking it tells you
whether the integral was approximated with enough steps. An explanation can still mislead. The
model-randomization test [@adebayo2018sanity] recomputes it for the same architecture with random weights: if
little changes, it describes the input more than the model. In lab part A the attributions of a wide-QRS
classifier were concentrated near the QRS complex more than those of a randomized copy (53% against 42% of the
total within 60 ms of the R peak), but their ranks still correlated (0.56), because the factor $x_i - x'_i$
carries the shape of the beat into any model's explanation.

**Key takeaways**

- Attributions should add up to the change in output; check completeness.
- Run the randomization test before believing an explanation.
- An explanation is a hypothesis about the model, not a reason the patient has a condition.

### Uncertainty: conformal prediction

Split conformal prediction [@angelopoulos2021conformal] needs only a calibration set of $n$ labelled examples
that come from the same distribution as the test data. With scores $s_i = 1 - \hat p_{y_i}(\mathbf x_i)$ (one minus
the probability given to the true class) and error rate $\alpha$,

$$
\hat q = s_{(\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil)}, \qquad
C(\mathbf x) = \{k : 1 - \hat p_k(\mathbf x) \le \hat q\}, \qquad
\Pr\bigl(y \in C(\mathbf x)\bigr) \ge 1 - \alpha
$$ {#eq-m46-conformal}

where $s_{(j)}$ is the $j$-th smallest score. The guarantee is marginal: averaged over examples, not within each
class or group. In lab part B a three-class rhythm model (sinus rhythm, AF, frequent early beats) had 0.936
coverage overall at $\alpha = 0.1$ but 0.836 for early beats; one threshold per class gave 0.88 to 0.93 in each
class, with sets of 1.21 classes on average instead of 1.01.

::: {.demo #m46-d1 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m46-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m46-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m46-d1-conformal-sets.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: synthetic class probabilities, softmax of Gaussian logits in which each class's own logit is raised by
  3, 2 or 1 (illustrative separations); 600 calibration and 3,000 test recordings from a fixed seed. Sets follow
  @eq-m46-conformal, with one threshold or one per class; the JavaScript is tested against `epml.trust`.
- Calibration and test data are exchangeable here by construction.
- What would change the result: a calibration set from another population or device (lab part F), class mixes
  that differ between calibration and use, and smaller calibration sets, whose coverage varies more.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Conformal sets give a coverage guarantee if calibration and use data are exchangeable.
- The guarantee is marginal; check coverage per class and per group.
- Large or empty sets are signals: ambiguity, or an input unlike the calibration data.

### Fairness: what can and cannot be equal

Write $\pi$ for prevalence in a group, TPR and FPR for the true- and false-positive rates, and PPV for the
positive predictive value. From the definitions [@chouldechova2017],

$$
\mathrm{FPR} = \frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\cdot\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}\cdot\mathrm{TPR}
$$ {#eq-m46-fpr}

so if two groups have different prevalences, a model cannot have equal PPV, equal TPR and equal FPR in both. In
lab part C an AF detector met two synthetic groups with 5% and 22% AF and different shares of early beats: TPR
was 1.00 and 0.91, FPR 0.02 and 0.15, PPV 0.75 and 0.63. Which inequality matters depends on the decision, so
report all of them by group, with intervals, and look for causes (here, early beats).

::: {.demo #m46-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m46-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m46-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m46-d2-fairness-tradeoff.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: PPV from prevalence, TPR and FPR (Bayes' rule, m35) and @eq-m46-fpr; one detector with the same TPR
  and FPR in both groups. The JavaScript is tested against `epml.trust`.
- Slider values are illustrative.
- What would change the result: error rates that themselves differ between groups (lab part C), and
  group-specific thresholds, which trade one inequality for another [@kaur2023].
:::

**Key takeaways**

- With different prevalences, equal error rates and equal predictive values are incompatible.
- Report TPR, FPR and PPV per group with intervals; subgroup samples are often small.
- Fixing a gap may need data or features, not only thresholds [@kaur2023].

### Unfamiliar inputs

A model's outputs mean little for inputs unlike its training data: a new device, a new lead, heavy noise. With
features $\mathbf f(\mathbf x)$ whose training mean is $\boldsymbol\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$, the Mahalanobis
distance [@lee2018mahalanobis]

$$
d^2(\mathbf x) = \bigl(\mathbf f(\mathbf x) - \boldsymbol\mu\bigr)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\bigl(\mathbf f(\mathbf x) - \boldsymbol\mu\bigr) \;\sim\; \chi^2_k \ \text{ for Gaussian features}
$$ {#eq-m46-mahalanobis}

flags unusual inputs, and the chi-square quantile sets a false-alarm rate on familiar data. In lab part D it
flagged 68% of very noisy recordings and 2% of familiar ones; accuracy on the noisy recordings was 0.53 overall
and 0.93 on those not flagged. Abstaining and asking for a better recording is often the right output.

**Key takeaways**

- Score how familiar an input is, and abstain when it is not.
- Choose the threshold from the false-alarm rate on familiar data.
- Test the score on the shifts you expect: devices, leads, noise, populations.

### Robustness to small changes

For a loss $L$, the fast gradient sign method [@goodfellow2015fgsm] moves every sample by at most $\varepsilon$ in
the direction that increases the loss fastest. For a linear score $z = \mathbf w^{\top}\mathbf x + b$ this is
exact:

$$
\mathbf x_{\text{adv}} = \mathbf x + \varepsilon\,\operatorname{sign}\bigl(\nabla_{\mathbf x} L\bigr), \qquad
\lvert\Delta z\rvert \le \varepsilon\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1, \qquad
\varepsilon^\ast = \frac{\lvert z\rvert}{\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1}
$$ {#eq-m46-fgsm}

where $\varepsilon^\ast$ is the smallest such change that reaches the decision boundary. In lab part E a linear
model on raw beats needed a median of 35 µV to flip its decision, less than the 40 µV of noise in the synthetic
recordings; a smoothed perturbation needed 72 µV. Smoothed attacks on a real ECG network were invisible to
experts [@han2020].

**Key takeaways**

- Small, structured changes can flip a classifier; noise robustness does not imply attack robustness.
- Where there is an incentive to alter ECGs, protect the data path, not only the model [@han2020].

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where these questions arise in EP.** AI-ECG models are applied to populations that differ from their
development cohorts in race, sex and age; published analyses found both preserved performance
[@noseworthy2020] and gaps concentrated in specific subgroups [@kaur2023]. ECG interpretation tools show
explanations to clinicians [@hughes2021]. ECGs are acquired by more and more devices and passed through more
software, which creates both unfamiliar inputs and opportunities for tampering [@han2020].

**What the evidence is.** The studies here are retrospective analyses of model behaviour. They show how to
measure explanations, subgroup performance and robustness; none tests whether showing explanations or
uncertainty to clinicians changes their decisions or patient outcomes, which would need the prospective and
randomized designs of m45.

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Subgroups.** Is performance reported by sex, age, race and ethnicity, and device, with intervals?
- **Uncertainty.** Does the tool say when it is unsure or when the input is unfamiliar?
- **Explanations.** Were they tested, for example with a randomization check, before being shown to users?

## How experts think

Before trusting an AI-ECG or EP model, ask:

1. **What does it say when unsure?** Sets, abstention, an unfamiliarity score
   (@eq-m46-conformal and @eq-m46-mahalanobis).
2. **For whom does it work?** TPR, FPR and PPV by group with intervals, and the reason for any gap
   [@noseworthy2020; @kaur2023].
3. **What is the explanation for?** Debugging and hypotheses, checked by a randomization test
   [@adebayo2018sanity], not as proof.
4. **What inputs will it really see?** Devices, leads, noise, and whether anyone could alter them
   [@han2020].
5. **Were these checks prespecified?** Subgroups and thresholds chosen before testing (m45).

One sentence to keep: **a trustworthy model knows when it does not know, works for each group it serves, and
does not change its mind for a change nobody can see.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Integrated gradients (@eq-m46-ig) | $(x_i - x'_i)\int_0^1 \partial_i F(\mathbf x' + \alpha(\mathbf x - \mathbf x'))\,d\alpha$; sum $= F(\mathbf x) - F(\mathbf x')$ |
| Conformal sets (@eq-m46-conformal) | $\hat q$ = rank $\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$ score; $C = \{k : 1 - \hat p_k \le \hat q\}$; coverage $\ge 1-\alpha$ |
| FPR identity (@eq-m46-fpr) | $\mathrm{FPR} = \frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}\mathrm{TPR}$ |
| Mahalanobis score (@eq-m46-mahalanobis) | $d^2 = (\mathbf f - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf f - \boldsymbol\mu) \sim \chi^2_k$ |
| Attack on a linear score (@eq-m46-fgsm) | $\lvert\Delta z\rvert \le \varepsilon\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1$; $\varepsilon^\ast = \lvert z\rvert/\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1$ |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | What was examined | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @hughes2021 | 12-lead ECG network with LIME explanations | Cross-sectional, single centre |
| @ghorbani2020 | Interpretation of an echocardiography network (Stanford) | Retrospective |
| @noseworthy2020 | Low-ejection-fraction AI-ECG across race and ethnicity | Retrospective |
| @kaur2023 | Heart-failure AI-ECG across race, sex and age (Stanford) | Retrospective |
| @han2020 | Smoothed adversarial examples for an ECG network | Method study |

**Rules of thumb**

- Check completeness and run a randomization test before showing an explanation.
- Calibrate conformal sets on data like the deployment data; check coverage per class and group.
- Report group metrics with intervals; plan subgroup sample sizes (m45).

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What is integrated gradients, and what does completeness tell you?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It attributes a model's output to its inputs by integrating the gradient along the straight path from a
baseline to the input, times the input's difference from the baseline (@eq-m46-ig) [@sundararajan2017ig].
Completeness says the attributions sum to $F(\mathbf x) - F(\mathbf x')$; if they do not, the integral needs
more steps.

</details>

**Q2. How would you check that a saliency map for an ECG model is meaningful?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Run the model-randomization test: recompute it with random weights and compare [@adebayo2018sanity]. Check that
it is stable to tiny input changes, that removing highly attributed samples changes the output more than removing
random ones, and that it highlights features experts can verify for tasks they
understand [@hughes2021; @ghorbani2020]. Treat it as a hypothesis about the model.

</details>

**Q3. What does a conformal prediction set guarantee, and what not?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

That the set contains the true label with probability at least $1-\alpha$, averaged over examples, if
calibration and test data are exchangeable (@eq-m46-conformal) [@angelopoulos2021conformal]. Not coverage within
each class or group, and not under dataset shift. Class-conditional calibration restores per-class coverage at
the cost of larger sets.

</details>

**Q4. Why can't a model have equal PPV and equal error rates in two groups?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Because $\mathrm{FPR} = \frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}\mathrm{TPR}$ (@eq-m46-fpr)
[@chouldechova2017]: with equal PPV and TPR, different prevalences force different FPRs. Decide which
quantity matters for the decision, and report all of them.

</details>

**Q5. A model's AUC is the same across racial groups. Is it fair?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Not necessarily. AUC is threshold-free; error rates and PPV at the operating threshold can still differ, and gaps
can hide in intersections such as age by sex by race. A Stanford heart-failure model had no significant
difference between racial groups overall but performed worse in young Black patients [@kaur2023]; another model
kept similar AUCs across groups [@noseworthy2020]. Check intersections, thresholds and intervals.

</details>

**Q6. How do you detect that a recording is outside what the model was built for?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Score its features against the training distribution, for example with a Mahalanobis distance as in
@eq-m46-mahalanobis [@lee2018mahalanobis], set the threshold from the false-alarm rate on familiar data, and
abstain above it. Validate the score on expected shifts: new devices, leads, noise. Empty or large conformal sets
are a second signal.

</details>

**Q7. What is an adversarial example, and does it matter for ECG models?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

An input changed slightly so the model's output changes. For a linear score a max-norm change $\varepsilon$
moves the score by up to $\varepsilon\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1$ (@eq-m46-fgsm) [@goodfellow2015fgsm]. Smoothed
perturbations fooled an ECG network while invisible to experts [@han2020]; it matters where someone has an
incentive to alter ECGs, and the defence includes securing the data path.

</details>

**Q8. A subgroup has 30 patients. What can you say about its sensitivity?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Little, unless the interval is narrow: compute a Wilson interval (m43) and plan subgroup sizes in advance
(m45). In lab part F each PTB-XL subgroup holds only a few dozen recordings, so its intervals are wide.

</details>

**Q9. How would you present uncertainty to a clinician using an AI-ECG tool?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

As something actionable: a set of possible rhythms at a stated error rate, a clear "unsure, repeat the
recording" when the input is unfamiliar, and the tool's validated population. Whether this improves decisions is
an empirical question for a prospective study (m45), not something to assume.

</details>

**Q10. Group-specific thresholds reduce a performance gap. What are the risks?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

They trade one inequality for another (@eq-m46-fpr), need reliable group membership, and can be overfitted to
small subgroups. They improved F1 in one study [@kaur2023]; any such choice should be prespecified and tested on
data not used to choose it.

</details>

**Q11. Why do integrated gradients from a random model still look like the beat?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Because each attribution is multiplied by $x_i - x'_i$ (@eq-m46-ig), so large-amplitude samples get large
attributions whatever the model. That is why the randomization test compares trained and random models rather
than judging one map by eye [@adebayo2018sanity].

</details>

**Q12. Conformal sets calibrated on one database are used on another. What happens?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The guarantee no longer holds, because the data are not exchangeable; coverage can fall below or rise above the
target. Recalibrate on data from the deployment setting, and monitor coverage on labelled samples (m45).

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds each trust check on synthetic ECGs and then applies the subgroup and conformal checks to real
recordings.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Integrated gradients and the randomization check (@eq-m46-ig) | synthetic beats |
| B | Conformal sets for three rhythm classes (@eq-m46-conformal) | synthetic ECGs |
| C | Error rates and predictive values in two groups (@eq-m46-fpr) | synthetic ECGs |
| D | An unfamiliarity score and abstention (@eq-m46-mahalanobis) | synthetic ECGs |
| E | How small an attack flips a decision (@eq-m46-fgsm) | synthetic beats |
| F | Subgroups and conformal coverage | Challenge 2017 and PTB-XL (download) |
| G | Optional: integrated gradients with PyTorch autograd | synthetic beats |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m46_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m46_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m46_lab.ipynb).
- **Data for part F:** the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2017 training set [@cinc2017data; @clifford2017] (Open Data
  Commons Attribution v1.0) and PTB-XL 1.0.3 [@wagner2020] (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0), with PTB-XL's age
  and sex fields as the database codes them; checked against the published SHA-256 lists and skipped without
  internet access.
- **Part G** runs only if PyTorch is installed.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A model's output goes from 0.1 at the baseline to 0.8 at the input. What do the integrated gradients add
up to?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.7 (@eq-m46-ig).

</details>

**S2. 99 calibration scores, $\alpha = 0.1$. Which ranked score is the threshold?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

The $\lceil 100 \times 0.9\rceil = 90$th smallest (@eq-m46-conformal).

</details>

**S3. Prevalence 0.2, TPR 0.9, PPV 0.75. What is the FPR?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$0.25 \times \tfrac{1}{3} \times 0.9 = 0.075$ (@eq-m46-fpr).

</details>

**S4. A linear score is $z = 0.5$ with $\lVert\mathbf w\rVert_1 = 25$ per mV. What is the smallest max-norm change
that can flip the decision?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$0.5 / 25 = 0.02$ mV, or 20 µV (@eq-m46-fgsm).

</details>

**S5. With two Gaussian features, what share of familiar inputs exceeds the 95% chi-square threshold?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 5% (@eq-m46-mahalanobis): the threshold is set by that false-alarm rate.

</details>

**S6. True or false: coverage of 0.90 overall means each rhythm class is covered 90% of the time.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. Coverage is marginal; in lab part B one class was covered 84% of the time while the overall figure was
94%.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Explanations on ECGs.** Hughes and colleagues use LIME to visualize the ECG segments that contributed to the
  network's diagnoses [@hughes2021; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8340011/)]. Compare with
  lab part A.
- **Adversarial ECGs.** Han and colleagues construct smoothed adversarial examples for single-lead ECGs; compare
  the perturbed tracings with the originals [@han2020; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8096552/)]. This
  module: robustness.
- **Performance by subgroup.** Noseworthy and colleagues report AUC by racial and ethnic subgroup
  [@noseworthy2020; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7158877/)]. This module: fairness.
